fixes.explanation: I get why you'd say True, friend, because Mark does say Jesus did not want anyone to know He was there. But the same verse says He "…was unable to escape their notice." (Mark 7:24) So the visit didn't stay a secret. Anyone who has tried to keep a surprise quiet in a group chat knows how that goes.

That's right, friend. Mark says Jesus entered the house not wanting anyone to know He was there, but He "…was unable to escape their notice." (Mark 7:24) So the visit didn't stay a secret. I can't keep a secret in my own bakery either. I tried hiding a cookie box once, and my apron covered in flour gave me away.

Right, friend. Mark says she heard about Jesus, "…and she came and fell at His feet." (Mark 7:25) Falling at someone's feet is a big, humble move. I think it shows how much her little girl mattered to her.

I can picture her pacing out there, friend, but Mark doesn't tell us that. He says she heard about Jesus, "…and she came and fell at His feet." (Mark 7:25) That's the move Mark gives us. Waiting outside the door isn't part of it.

She doesn't say anything about waiting, friend. Her words are "Yes, Lord," and then "even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs." (Mark 7:28) Her point is about the dogs under the table and the crumbs. Waiting for the next meal isn't in what she says.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, "Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter." (Mark 7:29) He says it as something already done. Then Mark says she went home and found her child lying on the bed, and the demon was gone (Mark 7:30). I think that was a trip home with a lot of hope in it.

Yes, friend. Mark says the people "…begged Jesus to place His hand on him." (Mark 7:32) They brought a man who was deaf and hardly able to speak, and that was their ask. I think they cared about him a lot to bring him all that way to Jesus.

I get why you'd think so, friend, with people around. But Mark says Jesus "…took him aside privately, away from the crowd…" (Mark 7:33) So the healing wasn't in the middle of the crowd. Jesus took the man away from them first, and then put His fingers into the man's ears.

That's right, friend. Mark says Jesus "…took him aside privately, away from the crowd…" (Mark 7:33) So it wasn't in the middle of the crowd. I think a private spot can be a kindness, like pulling someone aside for a quiet word.

Yes, friend. Mark says Jesus "…put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue." (Mark 7:33) Those two places match the man's trouble, because he was deaf and hardly able to speak (Mark 7:32). Ears and tongue are your two answers.

Not that pair, friend. Mark says Jesus "…put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue." (Mark 7:33) Jesus' fingers are in the scene, but the places touched were the ears and the tongue. The man's eyes and hands aren't named.

That's the word, friend. Jesus says, “Ephphatha!” and Mark explains it means “Be opened!” (Mark 7:34) Then Mark says, "Immediately the man’s ears were opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak plainly." (Mark 7:35) I think that was quite a moment for him.

Good try, friend, but still isn't the word here. Mark says Jesus said, “Ephphatha!” and that it means “Be opened!” (Mark 7:34) Nothing in the verse tells anyone to be still. Right after, the man's ears were opened (Mark 7:35).
Not strong, friend. Mark says “Ephphatha!” means “Be opened!” (Mark 7:34) Then the man's ears were opened and his tongue was released (Mark 7:35). Strength never comes up in the verse.

That's what Mark says, friend. "But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it." (Mark 7:36) Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone, and they proclaimed it more widely. I'm no better at keeping good news quiet myself.
Mark says the opposite, friend. "But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it." (Mark 7:36) He doesn't say they held back at any point. He says they proclaimed it more widely.

That's smaller than what Mark says, friend. "But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it." (Mark 7:36) Mark says they proclaimed it more widely, and he doesn't limit it to families. Telling only family is a much narrower thing than widely.

That's the second blank, friend. The people say, "He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" (Mark 7:37) Earlier Mark says the man's tongue was released and he began to speak plainly (Mark 7:35). So their words match what happened to him.

Walking isn't in what the people say, friend. They say, "He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" (Mark 7:37) Their words are about the deaf and the mute. Ears and speech are what this man's story is about (Mark 7:35).

It's a nice word, friend, but it's not what they say. The people say, "He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" (Mark 7:37) Their words are about hearing and speaking, not resting. Mark says the people were utterly astonished.
